q: How do I benchmark a steel supplier's carbon intensity: what is a good number for BF-BOF, DRI and scrap EAF routes?
title: Benchmarking a steel supplier's intensity
short: Compare the supplier against its own production route, not one global number. As labelled estimates, the world average is about 1.9 t CO2 per tonne of crude steel, blast furnace steel sits above 2, scrap based electric arc furnace steel sits well under 1, and coal based DRI is often higher than the blast furnace route.
audience: Steel buyers, EU importers, Indian auto and engineering firms

sections.h: Route ranges to start from (labelled estimates)
ul: Global average: about 1.9 t CO2 per t crude steel, from worldsteel's sustainability indicators. Check the latest year.
Blast furnace and basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF): typically about 2 to 2.5 t CO2 per t crude steel.
Scrap based electric arc furnace (EAF): well under 1 t, depending heavily on the grid factor of the electricity used.
Gas based DRI with EAF: usually between the two.
Coal based DRI, common in India: often above BF-BOF, because coal fired rotary kilns are less efficient.
p: These are ranges to spot outliers, not targets. A supplier far below its route's range should be able to explain why, for example renewable power, high scrap share or a narrow boundary.

sections.h: Make sure the numbers are comparable
ol: Same boundary: crude steel or finished product, and whether upstream steps such as pellets, coke, lime and oxygen are included.
Same gases and units: t CO2 or t CO2e per tonne.
Same electricity basis: location-based grid factor, or market-based with certificates.
Same year and same method: worldsteel, the CBAM method, or an EPD under ISO 14025.

p: In December 2024 the Ministry of Steel published a Taxonomy of Green Steel that rates steel by emission intensity per tonne of finished steel, with star ratings below about 2.2 t CO2e per tonne. Ask Indian suppliers whether they hold a rating and on what boundary. Thresholds and the rating process may be revised, so read the current text.

sections.h: Using CBAM default values as a ceiling
p: The EU publishes default embedded emission values for steel goods by CN code and country, with mark-ups that rise over the definitive period. A supplier with verified actual emissions below the default saves the importer CBAM cost, which makes the default a practical benchmark for EU-bound steel.

senseible: Senseible holds the supplier's fuel and electricity evidence and computes only from approved factors, so you can see what a supplier's own number rests on. It does not rate or rank suppliers or publish steel benchmarks.
